cards.summary: The Pragmatic Engineer's 2026 survey of staff-plus engineers found 63.5% active adoption, higher than any other experience tier. The hypothesis: senior engineers have enough context to verify AI output and catch errors, so they capture the productivity gain without the defect rate that makes juniors net-negative when using the same tools unsupervised. The implication is that AI tools compress the experience advantage rather than eliminate it.

cards.title: forEach Ignores async Callbacks — Your Awaits Are Silent No-Ops
cards.summary: Passing an async function to Array.forEach doesn't pause the loop. Each callback returns a Promise that forEach immediately discards, so iterations fire in parallel and unhandled rejections vanish silently.
cards.body: forEach was designed before async existed and simply calls your callback, ignoring whatever it returns. When you mark that callback async, it returns a Promise — but forEach throws it away, so the loop exits before any awaited work finishes. Errors thrown inside also go unhandled because there's no Promise chain to attach a .catch to. Swap to for...of when you need real sequential execution, or Promise.all when parallel is fine but you want to surface errors.

cards.title: CSS `fr` Units Share Free Space, Not Total Space
cards.summary: A `1fr` column is not "one fraction of the container width" — it is one fraction of whatever width remains after fixed tracks, gaps, and padding are subtracted. Mixing fr with px or gap changes every fr column's computed size.
cards.body: The browser first satisfies all non-flexible constraints: fixed pixel columns, minmax minimums, and gap. Only the leftover space — called free space — is divided among fr tracks according to their ratios. A grid that is 600px wide with a 20px gap and two columns of `1fr 1fr` gives each column 290px, not 300px. This is why replacing a px column with a larger one silently shrinks every fr sibling, even though you didn't touch those columns.

cards.title: EventEmitter Accumulates Listeners Silently Until the Array Grows Without Bound
cards.summary: Every `on()` call appends a closure to an internal array; if that code runs per-request rather than once at startup, listeners pile up and hold their captured scopes in memory indefinitely.
cards.body: Node emits a `MaxListenersExceededWarning` when a single event exceeds 10 listeners, but it is only a hint — the extra listeners still run and nothing is removed automatically. The real hazard is that each `on()` call pushes a new closure into an array owned by the emitter; if this happens inside per-request or per-connection setup code, the array grows with every request and each closure keeps its captured variables alive. The fix is `once()` for handlers that should fire once, or an explicit `off()` / `removeListener()` call paired with every `on()` when the lifecycle ends.

cards.title: A Mutable Default Argument Is One Object Shared Across Every Call That Omits It
cards.summary: Python evaluates default argument values once when the `def` statement runs, not on each call, so a list or dict default is the same object in memory for every caller that omits that argument.
cards.body: When Python compiles a function definition it evaluates all default expressions immediately and stores the resulting objects on the function itself. A list or dict default is therefore a single live object — mutations made inside one call persist and appear in the next, behaving like a hidden global variable attached to the function. The idiomatic fix is to default to `None` and construct the mutable inside the function body so each invocation gets its own fresh object.
cards.code:
def append_item(item, result=[]):  # 'result' is created once at def time
    result.append(item)
    return result

print(append_item(1))  # [1]
print(append_item(2))  # [1, 2]  ← not [2]

# Fix
def append_item(item, result=None):
    if result is None:
        result = []
    result.append(item)
    return result

cards.title: `Stream.parallel()` Submits to the JVM-Wide Common Pool — One Slow Task Blocks Everyone Else
cards.summary: `parallelStream()` and `Stream.parallel()` share `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` with every other parallel stream, library, and framework running in the same JVM process.
cards.body: `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` is a single, process-wide thread pool; any code that calls `parallelStream()` competes for the same workers, including third-party libraries and frameworks like Akka that use ForkJoin internally. A blocking operation inside a parallel stream — a slow database call, an HTTP request — pins a common-pool worker for its duration and can starve unrelated parallel work happening elsewhere in the process at the same time. When you need isolation, wrap the stream inside a dedicated `ForkJoinPool` submitted as a callable; the stream's tasks execute on that pool's threads rather than the common one.

cards.title: Not Deferring the `cancel` Func from `context.WithTimeout` Leaks a Timer Goroutine Per Call
cards.summary: `context.WithTimeout` starts an internal timer goroutine that runs until the deadline fires; skipping the returned `cancel` keeps that goroutine alive even after the operation finishes early.
cards.body: `context.WithTimeout` creates a child context backed by an internal timer goroutine that cancels the context when the deadline elapses. The returned `cancel` function stops that goroutine early; if you never call it, the goroutine lives until the timeout expires on its own — one leak per request that completes before its deadline. Under load the accumulation is steady and easy to miss in profiles because each goroutine is small and its lifetime is bounded only by the timeout duration. The Go documentation is explicit: defer `cancel` immediately after the call, unconditionally.

cards.title: A Read Replica May Not Yet Contain Your Own Committed Write
cards.summary: Replicas apply changes from the primary's write-ahead log asynchronously, so routing a read to a replica immediately after a write can return the value from before your commit — the replica simply hasn't replayed that transaction yet.
cards.body: Replication lag is usually milliseconds but spikes under heavy write load or network pressure, and during that window the replica genuinely does not have the data. This is the read-your-own-writes problem: a user saves a profile change and immediately sees their old name because the read was routed to a lagging replica. Common mitigations are: read from the primary for a short window after each write; record the primary's log sequence number at commit time and only read from replicas that have caught up to it; or route any read that must reflect a specific write directly to the primary.

cards.title: LSM-Tree Engines Make Writes Fast by Deferring the Cost to Background Compaction
cards.summary: LSM-tree databases buffer writes in memory and flush them sequentially to immutable files, eliminating random write I/O — but a continuous background compaction process rewrites those files and competes with live traffic for disk bandwidth.
cards.body: B-tree engines like Postgres update pages in place, which requires finding and overwriting an existing location on disk — inherently random I/O. LSM-tree engines like RocksDB, Cassandra, and LevelDB instead append every write to an in-memory buffer (memtable) and flush it as an immutable sorted file (SSTable) when the buffer fills; every flush is fully sequential regardless of key distribution. The deferred cost is compaction: a background process continuously merges and rewrites SSTables to reclaim space and maintain read performance, and its disk I/O competes with incoming writes and reads. Write-heavy workloads — time-series, event logs, metrics — favour the LSM write path; mixed or read-heavy workloads often prefer the simpler B-tree read path where data lives in one place.
cards.code:
# Write path comparison

# B-tree
client_write
  → find page on disk (random I/O)
  → update in place → fsync

# LSM-tree
client_write
  → append to memtable (RAM, microseconds)
  → flush to SSTable when full (sequential MB/s)
  → background compaction merges SSTables (competing I/O)

cards.title: What happens when you use a mutable default argument in a Python function, and why?
cards.summary: Tests whether the candidate understands that default argument values are evaluated once at function definition, not on each call.
cards.body: Python evaluates default argument expressions once — when the `def` statement executes — and attaches the resulting object to the function. So `def append(val, items=[])` creates one list object shared across every call that doesn't pass `items`. Each call that mutates `items` mutates that same shared list, which is why the list accumulates values between calls. The fix is to use `None` as a sentinel and create a fresh list inside the body: `if items is None: items = []`. This catches people because in most languages defaults feel like per-call initializers, but in Python they're one-time expressions bound to the function object. You can inspect the current default at any time via `append.__defaults__`, which returns the tuple of default values and lets you see the mutation in action.
followUps: How would you write a decorator that caches results, and would the same mutable-default trap apply to its cache dictionary?
If the default were an immutable object like a frozenset, would the same accumulation problem occur? Why or why not?

cards.title: Why does setTimeout(fn, 0) not execute immediately, and what determines when the callback actually runs?
cards.summary: Tests understanding of the browser event loop, the distinction between macrotasks and microtasks, and why 0 ms does not mean instant.
cards.body: `setTimeout(fn, 0)` places `fn` on the task queue (sometimes called the macrotask queue). The event loop can only pick up that task after the current call stack unwinds and all pending microtasks — resolved Promise callbacks, `queueMicrotask` callbacks, `MutationObserver` notifications — have drained. So even with a 0 ms delay, `fn` never runs until the synchronous code that scheduled it finishes. Browsers also clamp the delay to roughly 4 ms once `setTimeout` calls are nested beyond four levels deep. This means `Promise.resolve().then(g)` always fires before a `setTimeout(fn, 0)` scheduled at the same point, because microtasks drain completely before the loop pulls the next task. A rendering step (style, layout, paint) may also occur between tasks, which is why long chains of `setTimeout(fn, 0)` feel slower than equivalent microtask chains but don't block the UI the way a tight synchronous loop does.
followUps: If you schedule a requestAnimationFrame, a setTimeout(fn, 0), and a Promise.resolve().then(fn) in the same synchronous block, in what order do they fire and why?
Can flooding the microtask queue block rendering? What would that look like in practice?

cards.title: A user updates their profile, but when they immediately refresh the page they see the old data. Where could the staleness be hiding?
cards.summary: Tests whether the candidate can trace a read-after-write inconsistency through multiple caching and replication layers rather than blaming a single component.
cards.body: Staleness can hide in at least four layers. A CDN or reverse proxy may serve a cached GET response, so the update reached the database but the edge node never refetched. An application-level cache (Redis, Memcached) might still hold the old value if the write path didn't invalidate or update it. If the database uses read replicas, the read may hit a replica that hasn't received the latest write from the primary — this is ordinary replication lag. Finally, the browser itself may serve a stale response from its HTTP cache if `Cache-Control` headers are too permissive. Debugging starts by inspecting response headers (`Age`, `X-Cache`, `Cache-Control`) to rule out CDN and browser caching, then verifying application-cache TTLs, and checking replica-lag metrics. A common fix for user-facing reads is to route the writing user's own subsequent reads to the primary for a short window — a pattern called read-your-own-writes consistency.
followUps: How would you implement read-your-own-writes consistency without always routing to the primary and losing the read-scaling benefit of replicas?
If you invalidate the cache on write but the database transaction then rolls back, what inconsistency do you get and how do you guard against it?
What trade-off does setting Cache-Control: no-store on every profile response introduce, and when is it worth it?

cards.title: parseInt Meets Array.map
cards.summary: Array.map passes three arguments to its callback including the index, which parseInt interprets as the radix parameter — producing surprising results.
cards.code: console.log([10, 11, 12].map(parseInt));
cards.explanation: Array.prototype.map passes three arguments to its callback: the element, the index, and the array. parseInt accepts two: the string and the radix. So the calls become parseInt('10', 0), parseInt('11', 1), and parseInt('12', 2). Radix 0 defaults to base 10 giving 10, radix 1 is invalid giving NaN, and radix 2 parses only the leading '1' from '12' since '2' is not a valid binary digit, giving 1.

cards.title: Reading from a nil Map in Go
cards.summary: A nil map in Go returns the zero value on read without panicking — only writes to a nil map cause a runtime panic.
cards.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    var m map[string]int
    v, ok := m["key"]
    fmt.Println(v, ok)
}

options.label: panic: assignment to entry in nil map

cards.explanation: In Go, the zero value of a map type is nil. Reading from a nil map is perfectly safe — it returns the zero value for the value type and false for the comma-ok idiom, exactly like reading a missing key from an initialized map. Only writing to a nil map causes a panic. This lets you safely query a map variable you never initialized.

cards.title: Left-to-Right + with Mixed Types
cards.summary: Java's + operator evaluates left to right: numeric operands before a String are added arithmetically, but once a String operand appears, all subsequent + operations become concatenation.
cards.explanation: Java's + operator is evaluated left to right with equal precedence. First, 1 + 2 performs integer addition yielding 3. Then 3 + " hello " converts 3 to a String and concatenates, producing "3 hello ". From this point every + is string concatenation, so 3 and 4 are appended individually as "3" and "4", giving "3 hello 34". The wrong answers correspond to thinking all operations are concatenation, all are arithmetic outside the string, or a symmetric mix of both errors.

cards.title: split() vs split(' ') in Python
cards.summary: Python's argumentless split() collapses runs of whitespace and strips edges, while split(' ') treats every single space as a delimiter and preserves empty strings between them.
cards.code:
s = "  hello  world  "
a = s.split()
b = s.split(' ')
print(len(a), len(b))
cards.explanation: Calling str.split() with no arguments uses a special algorithm that splits on any whitespace, discards empty strings, and strips leading and trailing whitespace — yielding ['hello', 'world'] (length 2). Calling str.split(' ') treats each individual space as a separate delimiter, so consecutive spaces produce empty strings between them. For '  hello  world  ' that gives ['', '', 'hello', '', 'world', '', ''] — seven elements.

cards.title: Touch Event `preventDefault()` Silently Fails When the Listener Is Passive
cards.summary: Chrome and Firefox register `touchstart` and `touchmove` listeners as passive by default, so calling `preventDefault()` inside them is silently ignored — the browser logs a warning but never throws, making this nearly invisible in production builds where the console is closed.
cards.body: Browsers introduced passive listeners to unblock the compositor thread: if a touch listener might call `preventDefault()`, the browser must wait for your JS to finish before scrolling, killing 60 fps. To avoid that stall, Chrome 51+ made `touchstart` and `touchmove` passive by default on `window`, `document`, and `body`. When your handler calls `preventDefault()` on a passive listener, the scroll still fires, you get a console warning ('Unable to preventDefault inside passive event listener'), and nothing else — no exception, no visible failure path in your code. You must explicitly pass `{ passive: false }` to regain the ability to cancel the event, but know that doing so re-introduces the scroll latency the browser was trying to avoid.

cards.title: TypeScript's `satisfies` Operator Validates Without Widening Your Types
cards.summary: Annotating a value with `const x: SomeType = ...` forces TypeScript to widen the inferred type to `SomeType`, losing all literal precision. The `satisfies` operator validates the shape against the type while keeping the narrower inference — a critical difference when you downstream-use those literal types for routing, theming, or discriminated lookups.
cards.body: When you write `const palette: Theme = { primary: '#6366f1' }`, `palette.primary` becomes `string`, not `'#6366f1'`, because the annotation tells TypeScript to store the value as `Theme`. This is fine until you want to derive a union of valid colour values (`typeof palette[keyof typeof palette]`) — you get `string`, not a union of your actual hex literals. `satisfies` runs the same assignability check at the declaration site but leaves the inferred type alone, so downstream `typeof` queries see the real literals. This is especially sharp in config-driven codebases where you want both safety at the point of definition and precision everywhere the config is consumed.

cards.title: `scheduleAtFixedRate` Silently Cancels All Future Runs When a Task Throws
cards.summary: An unchecked exception thrown inside a `scheduleAtFixedRate` task permanently stops all future executions of that task with no log output and no thread termination — the only symptom is that your periodic work quietly disappears.
cards.body: The executor swallows the exception internally and marks the `ScheduledFuture` as failed; it will never reschedule the task. The thrown exception is accessible only by calling `.get()` on the returned future, which virtually no production code does. This is distinct from a thread crash — the executor and its other tasks continue running normally. Wrapping the entire task body in a `try/catch(Exception e)` is the only reliable guard.

cards.title: Appending to a Sub-Slice Writes Into the Original's Backing Array
cards.summary: A sub-slice shares its backing array with the original up to the original's capacity; `append` within that capacity overwrites elements the original slice still owns, with no allocation and no error.
cards.body: Slicing a slice with `s[low:high]` produces a new header pointing at the same array, with capacity extending to the end of the original — not just to `high`. Any `append` that does not exceed that capacity writes directly into the original's memory. The original slice's length is unchanged, so it still reads those positions, now with silently modified values. The three-index slice expression `s[low:high:max]` caps the sub-slice's capacity at `max`, forcing a new backing-array allocation on the first append beyond that limit.
cards.code:
original := []int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
sub := original[0:2]       // len=2, cap=5 — shares backing array

sub = append(sub, 99)      // within cap: writes to original[2], no alloc
fmt.Println(original)      // [1 2 99 4 5] — silently overwritten

// Three-index slice caps capacity, forcing alloc on next append:
sub2 := original[0:2:2]
sub2 = append(sub2, 99)
fmt.Println(original)      // [1 2 99 4 5] — unchanged

cards.title: One Non-Indexed SELECT Column Eliminates the Index-Only Scan
cards.summary: Every column in the SELECT list must exist in the index for the engine to avoid touching the heap; a single absent column forces a random-I/O heap fetch per matching row, erasing most of the index's benefit at scale.
cards.body: An index-only scan reads all projected data directly from the B-tree leaf pages, skipping the table heap entirely. The moment a query projects a column absent from the index, the planner must follow a row pointer back to the heap for each result row — converting sequential index reads into random page I/O that typically costs 10–100× more per row. In low-data or cache-warm environments this is invisible; the penalty emerges when your working set exceeds the buffer pool. PostgreSQL and SQL Server support an `INCLUDE` clause that adds non-key columns to leaf pages without widening the index key used for traversal, enabling coverage without affecting sort order or index size for inner nodes.

cards.title: Fanout-on-Write Amplifies Writes Linearly with Follower Count
cards.summary: Fanout-on-write delivers O(1) feed reads by writing a copy of every post to each follower's feed row at publish time, but an account with millions of followers produces millions of inserts per post — a burst that can overwhelm write capacity.
cards.body: The appeal of fanout-on-write is that reading a feed is a simple range scan on a pre-materialized table. The hidden cost is that write throughput must scale with the largest single account's follower count, not average follower count. A celebrity posting during a live event can issue tens of millions of queued inserts in seconds, which queues back-pressure across the entire write path. The standard mitigation is a hybrid: apply fanout-on-write for accounts below a follower threshold, and merge celebrity posts at read time (fanout-on-read) for accounts above it, capping worst-case write amplification per event at a controllable ceiling.

cards.title: Explain how Raft achieves consensus and what happens to in-flight client writes when the leader crashes mid-term.
cards.summary: Tests whether the candidate understands distributed consensus beyond buzzwords — log replication, commit semantics, and the split-brain window during leader election.
cards.body: Raft elects a single leader per term using randomized election timeouts; a candidate wins by receiving votes from a majority of nodes. The leader appends client writes to its log, replicates entries to followers, and marks an entry committed only once a majority has persisted it. When the leader crashes, followers that time out start a new election by incrementing their term. Any entries on the old leader's log that were not replicated to a majority are uncommitted and can be overwritten by the new leader's log. Clients whose writes were acknowledged before majority replication see those writes vanish — so production Raft systems pair writes with client-assigned idempotency keys and require linearizable reads to go through the leader's commit index. During a network partition, a stale leader in the minority partition can accept writes, but they never reach majority quorum and are rolled back when the partition heals.
followUps: How does Raft prevent a stale leader in a minority partition from serving linearizable reads that return data already overwritten by the new leader?
What is the practical difference between Raft's strong-leader model and Multi-Paxos, and when would you choose one over the other?
How does joint consensus work during a cluster membership change, and why can't you safely swap two nodes in a single configuration step?

cards.title: A component wrapped in React.memo still re-renders on every parent update. Walk me through every way memo can fail to bail out.
cards.summary: Tests whether the candidate understands React's shallow-comparison contract and the common patterns that silently defeat memoization.
cards.body: React.memo performs a shallow comparison of the previous and next props, and skips rendering only if every prop is referentially equal. It fails in several common ways. First, object or array literals in JSX (`style={{color:'red'}}`) create a fresh reference every render. Second, inline arrow functions passed as callbacks are new references unless stabilized with useCallback. Third, passing JSX as children creates new React element objects each render, which always fail shallow comparison. Fourth, if the component calls useContext, any change to that context's value triggers a re-render regardless of memo. Fifth, a buggy custom comparator passed as memo's second argument can silently return false. Diagnosis starts with React DevTools Profiler's 'Why did this render?' panel, which shows exactly which props changed. The fix is usually useMemo/useCallback for unstable references — but applying them everywhere adds overhead and complexity that can outweigh the render cost.
followUps: If you wrap every callback in useCallback and every object in useMemo, what's the cost, and when is that cure worse than the disease?
How does the React Compiler (React Forget) attempt to solve prop-stability automatically, and what patterns can it not optimize?
Why doesn't React.memo use deep comparison by default, and what would break if it did?

cards.title: Explain how backpressure works in Node.js streams — what highWaterMark controls, what ignoring a false from write() causes, and how pipe() handles it automatically.
cards.summary: Tests understanding of Node's stream flow-control mechanism and why ignoring it causes unbounded memory growth under production load.
cards.body: Every Writable stream has a highWaterMark that defines the byte threshold of its internal buffer. When `writable.write(chunk)` pushes the buffer past that threshold, it returns `false`, signaling the producer to pause. The producer should stop writing and wait for the `'drain'` event, which fires once the buffer flushes below the mark. Ignoring the `false` return lets data accumulate faster than the consumer can process it, growing the buffer without bound until the process OOMs. `pipe()` automates this: it calls `readable.pause()` when the writable returns `false` and `readable.resume()` on `'drain'`. For Transform streams, the same mechanism applies on both sides — the readable half can back-pressure the transform's internal processing. These bugs typically hide in development where local disk and loopback I/O are fast; they surface in production when a slow downstream destination (remote socket, saturated disk) falls behind the producer's throughput.
followUps: How does backpressure propagate through a pipeline of three or more piped streams, and what happens if a middle Transform buffers internally without respecting highWaterMark?
How does objectMode change the meaning of highWaterMark, and what traps does that create for streams processing variable-size objects?

cards.title: Tuple Augmented Assignment Trap
cards.summary: The += operator on a list inside a tuple mutates the list via __iadd__ before the tuple assignment fails.

options.label: TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment

cards.explanation: The += operator desugars to t[0] = t[0].__iadd__([3]). Python first calls __iadd__, which mutates the list in place to [1, 2, 3], then attempts the assignment back to the tuple slot, raising TypeError. Since the exception is caught and the list object was already modified, print shows [1, 2, 3].

cards.title: Object.is vs Strict Equality
cards.summary: Object.is and === diverge on exactly two edge cases: NaN self-equality and signed zero comparison.
cards.code:
console.log(Object.is(NaN, NaN), NaN === NaN);
console.log(Object.is(0, -0), 0 === -0);
cards.explanation: Object.is uses the SameValue algorithm, which treats NaN as equal to itself (unlike ===, which follows IEEE 754) and distinguishes +0 from -0 (unlike ===, which considers them equal). These are the only two cases where Object.is and === produce different results.

cards.title: Go String Length: Bytes vs Runes
cards.summary: Go's len() on a string counts bytes, not characters, which diverges from rune count for multi-byte UTF-8.
cards.explanation: In Go, len() on a string returns the byte count, not Unicode code points. The string "café" is 5 bytes because 'é' (U+00E9) requires 2 bytes in UTF-8, while the other three characters are single-byte ASCII. Converting to []rune yields the code point count of 4, one per visible character.

cards.title: Ternary Numeric Promotion
cards.summary: Java's ternary operator applies binary numeric promotion when both branches are boxed numeric types, silently widening the result.
cards.explanation: JLS §15.25.2 classifies this as a numeric conditional expression because both operands are boxed numeric types. Java unboxes Integer to int and Double to double, then applies binary numeric promotion, widening int to double. The result is 1.0, which gets autoboxed to Double when assigned to Object.

cards.title: Flex Children Won't Shrink Below Their Content Size — Until You Add `min-width: 0`
cards.summary: Flex items default to `min-width: auto`, which means the browser treats the item's intrinsic content size as its minimum. A child with a long word, a pre block, or a wide SVG will blow out the container rather than shrink, even with `flex: 1` applied. Setting `min-width: 0` on the child removes that floor and lets flexbox actually compress it.
cards.body: The flexbox spec intentionally sets `min-width: auto` on flex items so that content like text isn't silently clipped by default — a well-meaning default that becomes a trap in real layouts. The confusion is that `flex-shrink` still applies, but it can only shrink the item down to its min-width, not below it. This is why `overflow: hidden` on the child alone doesn't help: the item is still as wide as its content, just hiding what spills. Adding `min-width: 0` tells the browser the item has no intrinsic floor, so the flex algorithm can compress it freely and text truncation, scroll, or overflow handling on the child actually kicks in.

cards.title: Native Event Listeners in `useEffect` Capture State at Registration — Not at Call Time
cards.summary: A `window.addEventListener` callback registered inside a `useEffect` with an empty dependency array forms a closure over the state values that existed when the effect ran — those values never update inside the handler. The idiomatic fix is to mirror the stateful value into a ref and read from `ref.current` inside the listener, keeping the registration stable while always seeing the latest data.
cards.body: React's re-render model replaces the entire component function scope each render, but a listener attached to `window` or a DOM node lives outside that lifecycle — it holds a reference to one specific closure forever. This is not a React bug; it's how JavaScript closures work, but it conflicts with the mental model of state being 'live'. The dependency-array escape hatch (adding state to the deps array) re-registers the listener on every change, which is often expensive and introduces race conditions with rapid updates. A ref doesn't trigger re-renders, so the effect stays mounted once and the callback reads `ref.current` synchronously at the moment of the event, which always reflects the latest render's value.

cards.title: `Buffer.allocUnsafe` Skips Zeroing and Exposes Old Heap Memory
cards.summary: `Buffer.allocUnsafe` returns a memory segment without clearing it first, so the bytes contain whatever data previously occupied that address — prior request payloads, tokens, or session secrets. It is only safe when your code overwrites every byte before the buffer escapes the function.
cards.body: `Buffer.alloc(n)` zero-fills before returning; `Buffer.allocUnsafe(n)` skips that step for throughput. The memory you receive belonged to a previous allocation and retains its old contents. Sending or logging that buffer without fully overwriting it is an information-disclosure vulnerability, not just a correctness bug. The performance difference matters only for large, short-lived scratch buffers where you control every write.

cards.title: `logging.basicConfig` Is a Silent No-Op Once Any Handler Exists
cards.summary: `basicConfig` inspects the root logger for existing handlers and returns immediately if it finds any, so any library that touches the logging system before your call silently wins the configuration race. The fix is to call `basicConfig` before importing third-party code, or replace it with `logging.config.dictConfig`, which applies unconditionally.
cards.body: The root logger starts with no handlers; the first call to `basicConfig` configures it. But many libraries — and even a bare `logging.warning()` call earlier in the file — trigger lazy handler attachment. After that, every subsequent `basicConfig` call is a no-op, including yours. Because the function returns `None` either way, there is no error or warning to signal that your format, level, and output destination were ignored.
cards.code:
import logging
import third_party_lib  # adds a StreamHandler to root logger on import

# Silent no-op — root logger already has handlers
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")

# Fix: configure before any import that touches logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)
import third_party_lib  # noqa: E402

cards.title: `CompletableFuture.thenApply` Runs on the Thread That Calls `complete()`
cards.summary: Without an explicit executor, `.thenApply` callbacks execute on whichever thread completes the future — typically a Netty I/O thread or a JDBC connection-pool thread — not a thread you own or size for CPU work. Any blocking or CPU-intensive logic in that callback starves the framework thread that drives all other in-flight requests.
cards.body: The contract is: if the future is already done when the callback is registered, the registering thread runs it; otherwise the completing thread does. In practice this means a database driver thread or an event-loop thread silently absorbs your business logic. `.thenApplyAsync(fn, executor)` with an explicit `ExecutorService` hands the callback off to a pool you control and size independently of the I/O layer.

cards.title: `json.Unmarshal` into `interface{}` Silently Rounds Large Integers
cards.summary: Go's JSON decoder represents every number as `float64` when the target type is `interface{}`, and `float64` can only represent integers exactly up to 2^53 — so Snowflake IDs, nanosecond timestamps, and 64-bit database primary keys are silently rounded before your code ever sees them. Using `json.Decoder` with `UseNumber()` preserves the raw string and lets you parse it as `int64` without loss.
cards.body: The decoder chooses `float64` because it must pick a concrete Go type and the JSON spec treats all numbers identically. Values above 9,007,199,254,740,992 map to the nearest representable double, which can differ from the original by hundreds or thousands — enough to point to a different database row. The bug is silent: the rounded value is a valid `float64`, so no error is returned and no overflow flag is set.
cards.code:
data := []byte(`{"id": 9007199254740993}`) // 2^53 + 1
var m map[string]interface{}
json.Unmarshal(data, &m)
fmt.Println(m["id"]) // 9.007199254740992e+15 — wrong

dec := json.NewDecoder(bytes.NewReader(data))
dec.UseNumber()
dec.Decode(&m)
n, _ := m["id"].(json.Number).Int64()
fmt.Println(n) // 9007199254740993 — correct

cards.title: Two-Phase Commit Blocks Indefinitely When the Coordinator Crashes Mid-Protocol
cards.summary: Once a participant votes yes in phase one, it must hold its locks and wait for the coordinator's COMMIT or ABORT — it cannot unilaterally resolve because another participant may have already received a decision. A coordinator crash between PREPARE and the final broadcast leaves every participant blocked with no safe way out until the coordinator recovers.
cards.body: The blocking problem is structural, not a bug: a yes vote is a promise to honor whatever the coordinator decides, so acting alone risks violating atomicity. Participants cannot ask peers for the decision because peers are equally ignorant. Rows locked by in-doubt transactions remain unavailable for the entire outage window. Protocols like Paxos-based commit (used in Spanner and CockroachDB) break the dependency on a single coordinator by requiring only a quorum, so a crashed node does not halt progress.
cards.code:
Coordinator → participants: PREPARE
Participants → coordinator:  VOTE YES   # locks acquired
Coordinator crashes here

# Participants cannot abort — a peer may have seen COMMIT
# Participants cannot commit — no coordinator decision received
# Locked rows stay unavailable until coordinator node recovers

cards.title: A Hot Key Always Routes to the Same Shard — Resharding Cannot Help
cards.summary: Hash-based sharding distributes keys evenly in aggregate, but a single key with outsized traffic always maps to one node; adding shards redistributes other keys but leaves the hot key on whichever shard its hash selects. The only remedies act on the key itself: read-through caching, write buffering, or artificially splitting it into N sub-keys that scatter across the ring.
cards.body: The problem is not uneven distribution — it is that a single logical entity generates unbounded load. A celebrity user, a viral product, or a trending counter is one key regardless of how many shards exist. Splitting the shard ring moves the hot key to a different node but keeps it singular. The N sub-key pattern trades read simplicity for write scalability: writers pick a random sub-key; readers fetch all N and aggregate. For counters this is exact; for caches it requires a merge step.
cards.code:
# trending:worldcup always hashes to shard 4
# Shard 4: 90,000 req/s  ← saturated
# Shards 1-3: ~500 req/s  ← idle

# Fix: stripe the key across N sub-keys
INCR trending:worldcup:{randint(0, N)}

# Read path: fetch all N sub-keys, sum client-side
values = [GET trending:worldcup:{i} for i in range(N)]
total = sum(int(v or 0) for v in values)

cards.title: Your service needs to join data owned by two different microservices. Walk me through your options and their trade-offs.
cards.summary: Tests whether the candidate understands the fundamental tension between service autonomy and cross-service querying, and can reason about consistency, latency, and operational cost for each approach.
cards.body: The simplest option is API composition: the calling service queries both services and joins in memory. This is easy to build but couples availability to both services and can't efficiently handle filters or pagination that span both datasets. Data replication via change data capture (CDC) copies one service's data into the other's read store as a projection; this enables local joins with fast queries but introduces replication lag and schema coupling. A shared materialized view in something like Elasticsearch lets you pre-compute the join, but adds infrastructure to operate and carries the same eventual-consistency trade-off as CDC. The right choice depends on query latency requirements, tolerable staleness, write-to-read ratio, and whether you can absorb the operational cost of a streaming pipeline. In practice most teams start with API composition and migrate to CDC only when latency or availability requirements force it.
followUps: How would you handle the CDC consumer falling behind so the materialized view is stale by minutes instead of seconds?
What happens if Service A hard-deletes a record but Service B's projection still references it — and a user queries for it?
How would you efficiently support a cross-service filter like 'orders over $100 from users in Europe' without scanning both full datasets?

cards.title: Explain what happens during React hydration, why a server/client mismatch is dangerous, and how you'd debug one that only appears in production.
cards.summary: Tests understanding of the hydration contract between server-rendered DOM and client-side React, and practical debugging skills for SSR frameworks like Next.js.
cards.body: During hydration React walks the existing server-rendered DOM and attaches event listeners and fiber state to the nodes rather than creating new ones. It assumes the DOM structure exactly matches what the client's first render would produce. When there's a mismatch — a component reads window.innerWidth or Date.now() during render — React in dev mode warns and patches the DOM, but in production it silently patches or, in React 18+, can fall back to full client rendering for the mismatched subtree, causing a content flash and negating SSR performance gains. Production-only mismatches typically stem from browser APIs, locale-dependent formatting, or non-deterministic data fetching that returns different results on server vs client. To debug, compare the raw server HTML (via curl or view-source) against what the client's first render produces with identical props, and hunt for components that branch on client-only state. The fix is to defer client-only values to useEffect so the first render is deterministic, or use suppressHydrationWarning for intentionally dynamic content like relative timestamps.
followUps: What's the performance cost when React falls back to client rendering for an entire subtree during hydration?
How does React 18's selective hydration with Suspense boundaries change the blast radius of a mismatch?

cards.title: Explain how Go channels work internally — what data structure backs them, what happens on a send to a full channel, and why an unbuffered channel isn't just a buffer of size zero.
cards.summary: Tests whether the candidate understands channel mechanics beyond the API: the hchan struct, goroutine parking via sudog queues, and the direct-send optimization that makes unbuffered channels a true synchronization primitive.
cards.body: A channel is backed by an hchan struct containing a circular ring buffer (for buffered channels), a lock, and two wait queues — recvq and sendq — of sudog entries that represent parked goroutines. When a goroutine sends on a full buffered channel, the runtime enqueues a sudog onto sendq and calls gopark, which removes the goroutine from the scheduler's run queue until a receiver dequeues an element and wakes it via goready. An unbuffered channel has a zero-length buffer, but the critical difference is the direct-send optimization: when a receiver is already waiting in recvq, the runtime copies the value directly from the sender's stack into the receiver's stack frame without ever touching the buffer, then wakes the receiver. This means the send doesn't complete until a receiver accepts the value, making unbuffered channels a synchronization point — not merely a data pipe. This is why an unbuffered send happens-before the corresponding receive completes, a guarantee buffered channels only provide at the granularity of buffer transitions.
followUps: What happens if you close a channel that still has goroutines blocked in sendq?
Why does a select statement with multiple ready cases choose one pseudo-randomly, and what bug does that prevent?
How does the runtime avoid the lock entirely in the fast path of a send on a buffered channel with space available?

cards.title: Generator Return vs Yield in Spread
cards.summary: Tests whether a generator's return value is included when spreading into an array.
cards.explanation: The spread operator consumes the iterator by calling next() until done is true. A return statement produces { value: 3, done: true }, but iteration consumers like spread and for-of discard the value when done is true. Only yielded values (1 and 2) are collected into the resulting array.

cards.title: Python for-else Control Flow
cards.summary: Tests understanding of when Python's for-else block executes relative to break.
cards.explanation: Python's for-else runs the else block only when the loop completes without hitting a break. In the first call, no item is 0, so the loop finishes normally and else returns "no zero". In the second call, break fires on 0, skipping else and falling through to "found zero".

cards.title: Go Nil Pointer in Non-Nil Interface
cards.summary: Tests whether a nil concrete pointer assigned to an interface produces a nil interface value.
cards.explanation: A Go interface value is nil only when both its type and value components are nil. Here f() returns a nil *Err pointer, but assigning it to the error interface creates an interface with type=*Err and value=nil. Since the type component is non-nil, e == nil evaluates to false.

cards.title: Java Return Inside finally Block
cards.summary: Tests whether a return statement in a finally block overrides a return in the try block.
cards.explanation: The finally block always executes, even when the try block contains a return. When finally has its own return statement, it overwrites the pending return value from try. The JVM discards the try block's return value of 1, and the method returns 2 from the finally block instead.

cards.title: CSS `transform` on an Ancestor Silently Breaks `position: fixed`
cards.summary: Adding a CSS transform to any ancestor element creates a new containing block, causing `position: fixed` children to position relative to that ancestor instead of the viewport — a spec-compliant behavior that routinely breaks modals and tooltips when animations are added later.
cards.body: The CSS spec defines that `transform`, `filter`, `perspective`, `backdrop-filter`, or `will-change` with any of those values causes an element to establish a containing block for all descendants — including fixed-positioned ones. This means a `position: fixed` tooltip inside an animated card wrapper is no longer anchored to the viewport at all. The bug typically surfaces when a designer adds a hover animation (`transform: scale(1.02)`) to a card that happens to contain a dropdown or tooltip, and those elements suddenly jump to wrong positions. The only reliable fix is to move fixed-positioned overlays outside the transformed subtree in the DOM, often via a portal.

cards.title: TypeScript's Excess Property Check Is Bypassed by Intermediate Variables
cards.summary: TypeScript only runs excess property checking when an object literal is assigned directly to a typed target; assigning via an intermediate variable silently drops the check, meaning typo'd or unknown keys are accepted without error.
cards.body: Excess property checking is a special syntactic rule that fires only on fresh object literals at the point of assignment — it is not part of structural type compatibility. When you store an object literal in an intermediate `const` first, TypeScript widens it to its inferred type and then checks structural compatibility only, which does not flag extra properties. This is why a misspelled option key (e.g., `retries` on a type that expects `retry`) can silently pass through and be ignored at runtime with zero compiler feedback. The practical implication: wrapper functions that accept `options: SomeConfig` will not catch extra keys if callers build their options object separately before passing it.

cards.title: Node.js `cluster` Workers Have Independent Heaps — In-Process State Never Syncs
cards.summary: The `cluster` module forks OS processes, not threads, so every worker starts with a copy of the heap and then diverges. Any in-memory structure — rate-limit counters, feature flags, session maps — becomes silently per-worker, multiplying your effective limits by the worker count.
cards.body: Node's `cluster.fork()` calls `fork(2)` under the hood, giving each worker a private address space. A `Map` that tracks request counts will count independently in each of your four workers, so a rate limit of 100 will actually allow 400 requests before any single worker rejects. This is the same reason sticky sessions exist: load balancers that don't pin a client may route the same user to a worker with no session state. Any coordination — rate limiting, distributed locks, pub/sub fan-out — needs an external store like Redis.

cards.title: `multiprocessing` `fork` Copies Open DB Connections into Child Processes
cards.summary: On Linux, Python's default `fork` start method clones the parent including any open sockets and database connection pools. Both parent and child then race to use the same underlying TCP stream, causing protocol corruption or ghost queries with no exception raised.
cards.body: When `multiprocessing.Pool` forks, the child process inherits file descriptors byte-for-byte, including SQLAlchemy engine pools, psycopg2 connections, and Redis sockets. The parent and child then both write to the same kernel socket buffer, interleaving protocol frames. The database sees malformed packets and may silently return wrong results, drop the connection, or deadlock. The safe fix is `multiprocessing.set_start_method('spawn')` (slower, clean slate) or disposing the engine in a pool initializer before any child work begins.
cards.code:
import multiprocessing
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text

engine = create_engine("postgresql+psycopg2://...")  # opened at import time

def worker(item_id):
    # engine's pool was copied from parent — parent and child share sockets
    with engine.connect() as conn:  # silently reuses corrupted fd
        return conn.execute(text("SELECT * FROM items WHERE id=:id"), {"id": item_id}).fetchone()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    multiprocessing.set_start_method("spawn")  # clean process, no inherited fds
    with multiprocessing.Pool(4) as pool:
        results = pool.map(worker, item_ids)

cards.title: `ThreadLocal` Values Persist Across Tasks in a Thread Pool
cards.summary: Thread pools reuse threads, so a `ThreadLocal` set during one task is still visible to the next task that runs on the same thread — potentially from a different user or tenant. The value is never cleared automatically; you must call `remove()` in a `finally` block.
cards.body: `ThreadLocal` storage lives on the `Thread` object itself and has no concept of task boundaries. When a request sets a security context, database tenant ID, or trace ID into a `ThreadLocal` and the request handler returns without calling `remove()`, the next `Runnable` dequeued by that thread picks up a stale value. This is how tenant data bleeds across requests in shared-pool architectures. Frameworks like Spring's `RequestContextHolder` handle cleanup for you inside the servlet lifecycle, but code outside that lifecycle — async tasks, custom `ExecutorService` submissions — does not get the same treatment.

cards.title: `time.After` Inside a Loop Leaks a New Timer on Every Iteration
cards.summary: `time.After` allocates a `time.Timer` internally each time it is called and that timer is not garbage-collected until it fires. In a `select` loop where another case regularly wins, you accumulate thousands of live timers that hold memory until their full duration elapses.
cards.body: The Go runtime parks each `time.After` channel in a min-heap until the deadline; it has no way to know you've moved on to the next loop iteration. In a high-throughput message loop with a five-second idle timeout, every message arrival that triggers the `msg` case leaves a five-second timer still ticking. Under load you can hold millions of goroutine-seconds of unreleased timers. The fix is to allocate one `time.NewTimer` before the loop and call `Reset` after each use, checking the channel drain requirement the Go docs spell out.

cards.title: Snapshot Isolation Allows Write Skew Even When Every Individual Read Looks Consistent
cards.summary: Under snapshot isolation (PostgreSQL's default), two concurrent transactions each see a consistent snapshot at their start time, so both can read the same rows, independently conclude an invariant holds, and each write different rows — with neither seeing the other's write. The invariant breaks at commit time.
cards.body: This anomaly is called write skew and it's distinct from a dirty read or non-repeatable read. The classic example: two transactions both check that at least one doctor is on call, each sees two doctors, and each removes one — leaving zero. Neither transaction did anything 'wrong' from its own snapshot's perspective. Preventing it requires `ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE`, which adds predicate locking and rolls back one of the conflicting transactions with a serialization error you must retry. `REPEATABLE READ` in Postgres is snapshot isolation and does not prevent write skew.
cards.code:
-- T1 and T2 run concurrently; both see alice=oncall, bob=oncall (count = 2)

-- T1
BEGIN; -- snapshot: alice ON, bob ON
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM doctors WHERE oncall; -- 2, safe to remove one
UPDATE doctors SET oncall = false WHERE name = 'alice';
COMMIT; -- succeeds

-- T2 (concurrent)
BEGIN; -- same snapshot: alice ON, bob ON
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM doctors WHERE oncall; -- still 2 in its snapshot
UPDATE doctors SET oncall = false WHERE name = 'bob';
COMMIT; -- also succeeds → 0 doctors on call

-- Fix:
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
-- one transaction will abort with SQLSTATE 40001; application must retry

cards.title: Publishing to a Message Broker After `COMMIT` Creates an Invisible Split-Brain Window
cards.summary: Calling `kafka.send()` or `rabbitmq.publish()` immediately after a successful database commit looks safe but creates a gap: a crash, OOM kill, or network failure between the two writes leaves the DB updated with no event emitted and consumers permanently behind.
cards.body: The two operations — database commit and broker publish — cannot be wrapped in a single distributed transaction without a two-phase commit coordinator, which almost no production stack uses. The transactional outbox pattern sidesteps this by inserting the event as a row in an `outbox` table inside the same local transaction as the business write. A separate relay process (Debezium reading the WAL, or a polling job) reads committed outbox rows and publishes them, delivering at-least-once guarantees. Consumers deduplicate on an `event_id`. The relay is the only component that needs to be reliable; the application itself stays simple.

cards.title: A client retries a payment request after a network timeout, but the first request actually succeeded. How do you prevent the customer from being charged twice?
cards.summary: Tests whether the candidate treats idempotency as a first-class distributed-systems primitive — not just deduplication, but the storage, scoping, expiry, and concurrency tradeoffs of idempotency keys.
cards.body: Assign every mutation a client-generated idempotency key (typically a UUID) and store it atomically alongside the result in the same database transaction that processes the payment. Before executing, look up the key: if it exists, return the stored response without re-executing. Keys must be scoped narrowly (e.g., per-account) for fast lookups and given a TTL so the key store doesn't grow unbounded. The critical detail is that the key write and the side-effecting write must share a transaction boundary — if they're in separate stores, a crash between them re-opens the double-charge window. For downstream exactly-once delivery, pair this with the transactional outbox pattern: write the event to an outbox table in the same commit, then relay it asynchronously via a change-data-capture process. This design makes retries safe at every layer — client, load balancer, and internal service calls.
followUps: What happens if two retries carrying the same idempotency key arrive concurrently? How do you serialize them without a global lock?
How would you maintain idempotency guarantees across a saga that spans three independently-owned services?
If you use a TTL to expire idempotency keys, what specific failure mode does that reintroduce, and how do you mitigate it?

cards.title: Explain why adding threads to a CPU-bound Python workload can reduce throughput below single-threaded performance, and walk me through how you'd saturate all cores.
cards.summary: Tests whether the candidate understands the GIL's actual contention mechanics — the convoy effect, the switch interval, and the real-world alternatives — rather than just knowing the GIL exists.
cards.body: CPython's Global Interpreter Lock permits only one thread to execute bytecode at a time. For CPU-bound work, multiple threads compete for the GIL every 5 ms (the default switch interval), and the overhead of releasing, signaling, and re-acquiring the lock creates a convoy effect that makes multi-threaded code measurably slower than a single thread. I/O-bound threads dodge this because they release the GIL before entering a blocking syscall. For true CPU parallelism you have three main options: multiprocessing (separate interpreters with separate GILs, at the cost of IPC serialization), C extensions that release the GIL explicitly (NumPy, Cython with nogil blocks), or a ProcessPoolExecutor that gives you a clean futures-based API over process-level parallelism. Python 3.13 shipped an experimental free-threaded build (PEP 703) that removes the GIL entirely, but every C extension must be audited for thread safety, so production adoption is still narrow.
followUps: Why does the GIL not affect I/O-bound threads — what specific mechanism releases it during a socket read or file write?
What are the concrete tradeoffs between multiprocessing with shared memory, a ProcessPoolExecutor, and Cython nogil blocks for a NumPy-heavy pipeline?

cards.title: Explain what a happens-before relationship means in the Java Memory Model and why declaring a field volatile doesn't make check-then-act operations thread-safe.
cards.summary: Tests whether the candidate distinguishes visibility guarantees from atomicity — the exact confusion that produces the majority of Java concurrency bugs in production.
cards.body: A happens-before relationship is a partial ordering guarantee: if action A happens-before action B, then A's memory effects are visible to B. Writing to a volatile field happens-before every subsequent read of that same field, which prevents both stale reads and compiler/CPU reordering across the volatile access. However, volatile provides visibility and ordering only — not atomicity of compound operations. A check-then-act sequence like `if (!flag) { flag = true; doWork(); }` is still a data race: two threads can both observe `false` before either completes the write. To make the compound operation indivisible you need a CAS-based atomic (AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet), a synchronized block, or a Lock. The broader principle is that the JMM defines when writes become visible, not when sequences of reads and writes are mutually exclusive — confusing these two properties is the root cause of most lock-free bugs.
followUps: How does the happens-before chain extend through a ReentrantLock's lock and unlock versus a volatile read and write — are they equivalent in ordering strength?
Describe a realistic scenario where a non-volatile long field is torn on a 32-bit JVM, even though individual word-sized writes are atomic.
When would you prefer a plain volatile boolean over AtomicBoolean, and what do you lose by choosing it?

cards.title: Python Short-Circuit Return Values
cards.summary: Python's `or` and `and` operators return the operand that determined the result, not a boolean.
cards.code:
a = 0 or "" or [] or "hello" or 42
b = 1 and "world" and [] and "foo"
print(a, b)
cards.explanation: Python's `or` returns the first truthy operand (or the last if all are falsy), while `and` returns the first falsy operand (or the last if all are truthy). For `a`, the chain skips 0, "", and [] (all falsy) and returns "hello" — the first truthy value — without ever reaching 42. For `b`, 1 and "world" are truthy, but [] is falsy, so `and` short-circuits and returns [].

cards.title: Array.sort Default Comparison
cards.summary: JavaScript's Array.sort without a comparator converts elements to strings and sorts lexicographically, not numerically.
cards.explanation: When no comparator is supplied, Array.prototype.sort converts each element to a string and compares by UTF-16 code unit order. The string representations are "10", "100", "70", "8", and "9". Lexicographically, "10" < "100" < "70" < "8" < "9" because comparison proceeds character by character, and the code point for '1' is less than '7', which is less than '8'.

cards.title: Go iota with Blank Identifier
cards.summary: Using `_` in a Go const block with iota consumes the counter value without creating a named constant.
cards.explanation: In a Go const block, iota increments by 1 for each constant specification regardless of whether the name is used or discarded. The expression `iota * 2` is implicitly repeated for every subsequent line. A = 0×2 = 0, B = 1×2 = 2, C = 2×2 = 4, the blank identifier _ consumes iota = 3 (value 6, discarded), and D gets iota = 4 so D = 4×2 = 8.

cards.title: Java Switch Fall-Through
cards.summary: Without `break` statements, Java's switch falls through every subsequent case and default after the first match.
cards.explanation: Java's switch statement falls through all subsequent cases once a match is found unless an explicit `break` is encountered. After matching case 1, execution continues unconditionally through case 2, case 3, and default. The accumulation is y = 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. The option 6 corresponds to the wrong belief that `default` is skipped during fall-through; the option 1 corresponds to assuming each case has an implicit break.

cards.title: position: sticky Breaks Silently When an Ancestor Has overflow: hidden
cards.summary: Any ancestor with overflow: hidden, auto, or scroll becomes a scroll container, constraining sticky positioning to that box — which is almost never what you want. Swapping to overflow: clip preserves visual clipping without creating a scroll container.
cards.body: Sticky positioning works by anchoring an element relative to its nearest scrollable ancestor. When a wrapper anywhere up the DOM tree has overflow: hidden, the browser silently promotes that element to the scroll container, so position: sticky is scoped to a box that may never scroll. The element doesn't warn you — it just behaves like position: relative. The fix is overflow: clip, which was designed exactly for this: it clips painted overflow without establishing a new scroll container, so sticky elements can find the real viewport scroller.

cards.title: Object.keys() Returns string[], Not (keyof T)[] — and That's Correct
cards.summary: TypeScript intentionally widens Object.keys() to string[] because structural typing lets objects carry undeclared properties at runtime, making a narrower return type unsound. A typed wrapper trades that soundness warning for ergonomics — know where you're accepting the risk.
cards.body: TypeScript's type system is structural, not nominal: a value typed as { host: string; port: number } may at runtime have additional keys. Returning (keyof T)[] from Object.keys would imply you know every key, which TypeScript cannot guarantee. Casting through a typedKeys helper localises the unsoundness to one place rather than scattering as (keyof T) casts across the codebase. This pattern is safe for objects you construct and own; avoid it for function parameters where callers may pass supertypes.

cards.title: `.pipe()` Silently Abandons Streams on Error
cards.summary: When a stage in a `.pipe()` chain emits an error, Node stops moving data but leaves every other stream open — file handles, sockets, and transform buffers all remain uncollected. `stream.pipeline` wires shared error listeners across every stage and calls `.destroy()` on all of them on the first failure.
cards.body: `.pipe()` listens only for the destination's `end` event and has no built-in error forwarding between stages. An error on a Transform propagates nowhere: the source readable stalls (not closed) and the destination writable stays open, leaking the underlying resource. `stream.pipeline` solves both issues by attaching error listeners to every stream in the chain and destroying all of them on any error. Use `require('stream/promises').pipeline` (Node 15+) to get a promise-returning version that also handles async generators cleanly.

cards.title: `@lru_cache` on Instance Methods Leaks Every Instance
cards.summary: `lru_cache` treats `self` as part of the cache key and holds a strong reference to it, so every object that ever calls the decorated method is pinned in memory for the cache's lifetime — the instance's `__del__` never fires and the GC cannot reclaim it.
cards.body: The decorator stores `(self, *args)` tuples in an internal dict, and dicts hold strong references. Because the cache lives on the class (not the instance), it remains reachable as long as the class itself is loaded — which in practice means forever. For per-instance memoization, `functools.cached_property` stores results directly in the instance's `__dict__`, so they are collected with the instance. For shared memoization, lift the computation to a module-level function that takes only primitive values and cache that instead.

cards.title: `synchronized` Pins Virtual Threads and Kills Loom's Scalability
cards.summary: When a virtual thread enters a `synchronized` block or method, the JVM pins it to its carrier (platform) thread — it cannot unmount even while blocking on I/O. Any blocking call inside a monitor holds a real OS thread, collapsing the scalability benefit of Project Loom.
cards.body: Virtual threads gain their efficiency by unmounting from carrier threads during blocking operations so the carrier can run other virtual threads. `synchronized` uses JVM object monitors, which are bound to carrier-thread identity; the runtime cannot unmount a virtual thread that owns one. Old JDBC drivers, legacy crypto libraries, and any code with blocking I/O inside `synchronized` all trigger pinning. Replace monitors with `ReentrantLock`, which parks cooperatively and allows unmounting. On JDK 21+ you can detect pinning with `-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full` or by watching the `jdk.VirtualThreadPinned` JFR event.

cards.title: `http.DefaultClient` Has No Timeout — Goroutines Block Forever
cards.summary: `http.DefaultClient` sets `Timeout` to zero, disabling all deadlines. A server that accepts the TCP connection but never sends a response holds your goroutine open indefinitely, and in a service under load this silently exhausts the goroutine pool or file-descriptor limit.
cards.body: `http.Client.Timeout` covers the entire round-trip: dial, TLS handshake, request write, redirect follows, and reading the full response body. Zero means no limit at any stage. The default client is a shared package-level variable used by `http.Get`, `http.Post`, and friends — one stalled upstream can starve unrelated calls that share the same transport's connection pool. Always construct a named `http.Client` with `Timeout` set. If you need finer control, configure `Transport.DialContext`, `ResponseHeaderTimeout`, and `IdleConnTimeout` separately.

cards.title: Write-Behind Caching Silently Loses Acknowledged Writes on Failure
cards.summary: Write-behind (write-back) caches acknowledge the client write immediately and flush to the database asynchronously — if the cache node crashes before the flush, those writes vanish with no error ever returned to the caller and no record in the DB.
cards.body: The throughput appeal of write-behind is real: batching and coalescing writes before hitting durable storage reduces DB pressure dramatically. The hidden cost is that the cache becomes the system of record for all unflushed mutations, so its durability guarantees now matter as much as the database's. Redis with `appendfsync everysec` (the default AOF mode) can lose up to one second of writes on a crash — silently, because the client already received a success response. Mitigations include `appendfsync always` (serializes all writes through the OS, largely negating the throughput win), using a durable queue like Kafka as the write buffer instead of Redis alone, or reserving write-behind only for genuinely loss-tolerant data such as view counters.
cards.code:
# redis.conf defaults — a crash can drop up to 1 second of acknowledged writes
appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec

# Zero data-loss option — fsync on every write, but kills throughput
# appendfsync always

# Durable alternative: write to Kafka first, consume into DB async
# Cache reflects the committed log, not unsynced memory

cards.title: Modulo Sharding Remaps Nearly Every Key When You Rescale
cards.summary: With `hash(key) % N` sharding, adding one node changes N and therefore reassigns roughly `(N-1)/N` of all keys to different shards — invalidating your entire cache or forcing a full data migration. Consistent hashing limits remapping to approximately 1/N of keys.
cards.body: In a 10-node modulo cluster, `hash(k) % 10` and `hash(k) % 11` agree only when both results happen to be equal, which is about 9% of keys — so a scale-out event silently invalidates ~91% of your cache and thunders those misses straight to the database. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a hash ring; adding a node only steals keys from the arc between it and its predecessor. Without virtual nodes, though, physical placement on the ring is uneven and one node may own a disproportionate arc. Assign each physical node V virtual positions (100–150 is common) to smooth the distribution — this is the basis of memcached's ketama, Cassandra's token ranges, and most modern distributed KV stores.

cards.title: You need to enforce a global rate limit of 10,000 req/s across 20 stateless API gateway instances. Walk me through your design and its failure modes.
cards.summary: Tests whether the candidate understands distributed counting, the consistency-latency tradeoff in shared state, and graceful degradation when the coordination layer fails.
cards.body: The standard approach uses a centralized counter in Redis with a sliding-window algorithm—either a sorted set of timestamps or a fixed-window counter with interpolation between the current and previous window. Each gateway atomically increments via a Lua script and checks the result against the threshold. The critical failure mode is Redis going down: you need a fallback, typically a local token bucket per instance pre-loaded with its share of the global budget (500 req/s each). This sacrifices accuracy but prevents both open-flooding and hard-blocking all traffic. A subtler issue is burst traffic at window boundaries; the sliding-window-counter algorithm handles this by weighting the previous window's count, smoothing the edge. You must also address split-brain: if some gateways lose connectivity to Redis while others don't, enforcement becomes inconsistent. The design choice is whether to fail-open (risk over-admission) or fail-closed (risk dropping legitimate traffic), and that decision should be configurable per route.
followUps: How would you handle a sudden failure where 15 of 20 instances go down and the surviving 5 inherit all traffic—does your rate limit still hold?
What's the memory and accuracy tradeoff between a sliding-window-log and a fixed-window-counter approach at high throughput?
How would you extend this to per-tenant limits with 100,000 tenants without exploding your Redis keyspace?

cards.title: Explain how Go's runtime scheduler multiplexes goroutines onto OS threads and what happens when a goroutine makes a blocking system call.
cards.summary: Tests understanding of the GMP scheduling model, the hand-off mechanism for blocking syscalls, and how asynchronous preemption prevents compute-bound goroutines from monopolizing a thread.
cards.body: Go uses an M:N scheduler built around three entities: G (goroutine), M (OS thread), and P (logical processor, capped at GOMAXPROCS). Each P owns a local run queue of runnable Gs. When a goroutine enters a blocking syscall, the runtime performs a hand-off: it detaches the P from the blocked M and assigns it to an idle or newly spawned M so other goroutines keep running. When the syscall returns, the M tries to reacquire a P; if none are free, its G goes to the global run queue and the M parks. For network I/O, the runtime avoids this entirely—the netpoller uses epoll/kqueue to multiplex socket readiness, so network-blocked goroutines never consume an OS thread. Since Go 1.14, the scheduler emits SIGURG-based asynchronous preemption signals, allowing it to pause goroutines stuck in tight compute loops that lack cooperative preemption points. Work stealing across P run queues and periodic checks of the global queue ensure load balance without a centralized lock.
followUps: What class of bugs did non-preemptive scheduling cause before Go 1.14, and how does signal-based preemption solve them?
How does the netpoller integrate with the scheduler so that thousands of concurrent network connections don't each pin an OS thread?

cards.title: Explain how the browser promotes an element to its own compositing layer, what will-change: transform actually does at the rendering pipeline level, and why over-promoting hurts performance.
cards.summary: Tests whether the candidate understands the paint-to-composite pipeline separation and can reason about GPU memory tradeoffs rather than blindly applying optimization hacks.
cards.body: After layout and paint, the compositor decides which subtrees to rasterize into separate GPU-backed textures called layers. Properties like transform, opacity, and filter can be animated entirely on the compositor thread—but only if the element already lives on its own layer. Declaring will-change: transform tells the browser to eagerly promote the element, allocating a dedicated texture and rasterizing it independently. Subsequent transform animations then only require the compositor to reposition the texture, never touching the main thread or triggering repaint. The cost is concrete: every layer consumes GPU memory proportional to its pixel dimensions times device pixel ratio, and the compositor must composite all layers each frame. Over-promoting dozens of elements can exhaust VRAM, trigger fallback to software rasterization, or inflate composite time beyond the frame budget. The correct pattern is to apply will-change shortly before an animation begins and remove it on transitionend or animationend, so layers exist only while they deliver value.
followUps: How would you diagnose excessive layer promotion in DevTools, and which metrics tell you you've crossed the line?
Give an example of implicit layer promotion—where the browser creates a layer you didn't ask for—and explain why it happens.
Why can animating left or top never be compositor-only, even if the element is on its own layer?

cards.title: Closure Over `var` in a Loop
cards.summary: All three closures share the same function-scoped `var i`, which is 3 after the loop ends.
cards.explanation: Because `var` is function-scoped, there is a single `i` binding shared by all three closures. The loop exits when `i` reaches 3, so every closure returns 3. Using `let` instead would create a new binding per iteration, yielding 0, 1, 2.

cards.title: List Repetition and Shared References
cards.summary: The `*` operator on a list of lists copies references, not the inner objects, so mutating one element affects all of them.
cards.explanation: The expression `[[0]] * 3` creates a list containing three references to the same inner list object. Assigning `a[0][0] = 1` mutates that single inner list, and because all three slots point to it, the change is visible in every position. Use a list comprehension like `[[0] for _ in range(3)]` to get independent copies.

cards.title: Slice Append and Shared Backing Array
cards.summary: Appending to a sub-slice that still has capacity overwrites the original slice's backing array instead of allocating a new one.
cards.explanation: The slice literal `s` has len 3 and cap 3. The sub-slice `a = s[:2]` has len 2 but still cap 3, sharing the same backing array. Because there is remaining capacity, `append(a, 4)` writes 4 into the third position of that array, overwriting `s[2]`. A new backing array would only be allocated if `append` exceeded the capacity.

cards.title: Integer Autoboxing Cache Boundary
cards.summary: Java caches `Integer` objects for values −128 to 127; `==` on autoboxed values outside that range compares distinct object references.
cards.explanation: The JLS requires `Integer.valueOf` to cache values from −128 to 127. Autoboxing 127 returns the same cached object for both `a` and `b`, so `==` is true. Autoboxing 128 creates two separate `Integer` objects, so `==` compares references and returns false. Use `.equals()` for reliable value comparison across the full range.

cards.title: CSS `gap` Applies to Flex Containers Even When Items Don't Wrap
cards.summary: The `gap` property on a flex container adds space between items regardless of wrapping. Developers often assume it only matters in grid or multi-line flex layouts, then get burned when a single-row flex row has unexpected spacing that `margin` hacks can't cleanly override.
cards.body: Unlike margins, `gap` is owned by the container and distributes space strictly *between* items — never on the outer edges. This means you cannot accidentally create a leading or trailing gap, which is the exact bug that `* + * { margin-left }` tricks introduce. The catch: `gap` doesn't collapse with sibling margins the way block margins do, so mixing the two in the same axis produces additive spacing that's hard to debug.
